title: Review Evaluates AI and Quantum Computing Paradigms for Adaptive Combinatorial Optimization - Quantum Computing Report
gist: A review by Hoong Chuin Lau (Singapore Management University) of 119 papers finds AI-assisted quantum optimization shows clear benefits in cutting hardware calls and handling constraints, while quantum-assisted AI is largely unproven. No screened study reaches matched-resource hardware advantage, and many lack classical baselines.

insights.claim: A review of 119 papers (67 coded in detail) concludes AI-assisted quantum optimization shows clear benefits in reducing hardware calls and managing constraints, whereas quantum-assisted AI models remain largely unproven for practical advantage on current hardware.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Near-term commercial value in quantum optimization sits in AI-orchestrated hybrid workflows, not quantum-enhanced machine learning.

insights.claim: Zero studies in the screened corpus reach the top M5 maturity level (end-to-end hardware execution with matched-resource advantage), and the median experiment size is 16 qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: No demonstrated quantum advantage in this literature; claims of optimization advantage should be discounted until matched-resource hardware evidence appears.

insights.claim: The review proposes an M0-M5 evidence hierarchy running from conceptual mechanics and ideal statevector simulations (M0-M1), through cross-size generalization and noisy or hardware component testing (M2-M3), to end-to-end hardware execution and matched-resource advantage (M4-M5).
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Gives investors a checklist for grading vendor and academic claims by how far up the maturity ladder they actually are.

insights.claim: Quantum-for-AI research is concentrated at low maturity: 13 of 15 such papers stay at M1-M2, while AI-for-quantum-optimization is the most mature area at M2-M3, with examples such as parameter transfer and noise mitigation.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Quantum machine learning pitches rest on mostly simulated evidence; the more credible work is AI used to make quantum solvers cheaper and more robust.

insights.claim: 22 of 52 core studies included no classical baseline, so many reported quantum results cannot be judged against standard classical methods.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Over 40% of core studies lack a baseline, undermining the reliability of published quantum optimization performance claims.
insights.locator: The analysis finds that 22 out of 52

insights.claim: Only 10 of 24 applicable studies isolated the quantum contribution through proper ablation tests, leaving it unclear whether quantum components drive the reported gains.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Attribution of gains to the quantum component is unproven in most studies, a risk for firms marketing quantum-specific advantage.

insights.claim: Scaling quantum optimization is increasingly a systems engineering problem rather than a pure qubit-count challenge.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Value may accrue to compilers, encodings and workflow software layers rather than only to raw qubit-count hardware.
insights.quote: scaling quantum optimization is increasingly a systems engineering problem rather than a pure qubit-count challenge

insights.claim: Constraints, penalty weights, slack encodings, and transpiled two-qubit gate depths often dictate performance before circuit parameters are chosen.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Problem formulation and compilation overhead can dominate outcomes, so adding qubits alone will not guarantee better optimization results.

insights.claim: The review emphasizes selective quantum use: learned controllers that predict whether the marginal benefit of invoking a quantum processor outweighs its computational, sampling and queueing costs.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Points to a future of quantum as a selectively called accelerator, with orchestration and scheduling software as a value layer and queueing/access cost as a real constraint.
insights.locator: Consequently, the review emphasizes selective quantum use

insights.claim: The review defines three paradigms by where learning and quantum computation sit: AI-for-QO (AI tunes parameters, initialization or execution settings of a quantum solver), Q-for-AI (quantum layers embedded in machine learning models), and AI-Quantum Co-Optimization (learned policies dynamically allocating work between classical and quantum routines).
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A taxonomy for sorting quantum-AI startups and research claims into distinct maturity and value-capture buckets.
insights.locator: The review categorizes research into three distinct paradigms
